name: Administer medications on inpatient units
summary: This process covers one inpatient's medications for one day: the scheduled passes at about 08:00, 12:00, 17:00 and 22:00, as-needed doses, IV infusions and the overnight check of the medication record. The assigned nurse takes doses from the automated dispensing cabinet, checks them against the medication record, confirms the patient's identity, gives them and documents each one. It is slow and error-prone because every nurse on the unit does the same pass at the same time, interruptions are frequent, high-alert drugs need a second nurse, and missing doses mean calls to pharmacy.

baseline.org_archetype: A three-site Ontario community hospital with automated dispensing cabinets on inpatient units, an electronic or pharmacy-printed medication administration record and partial barcode scanning at the bedside.
baseline.notes: One case is one patient day. The steps use medicine-unit nurse roles to stand for the nurses of every inpatient unit; the role list allocates time to surgical, ICU, mental health, postpartum and paediatric nurses as well.

unit_of_work: one inpatient day of medication passes
trigger: A new hospital day begins for an admitted patient with active medication orders dispensed by pharmacy.
end_state: Every dose due in the day has been given, held with a reason or reported as an incident, and the 24-hour medication record is checked.

volume.seasonality: Follows inpatient occupancy: highest in winter respiratory season.

evidence.note: Organisation file estimate: one case per occupied bed day, 639 beds at 90-100% occupancy.

surge.cause: Winter respiratory season and COVID-19 waves (surge and field hospital beds open)

evidence.note: Author's estimate following the medicine program surge in the organisation file, diluted by surgical and maternity units that do not surge.

systems.name: Hospital information system (electronic patient record with ADT, order entry, results, eMAR and clinical documentation)
Pharmacy information system and automated dispensing cabinets
Safety incident and complaints reporting system
Email, telephone, pagers and wireless phones

steps.name: Review the medication record at the start of the shift
steps.description: At 07:00 the assigned nurse opens the patient's electronic medication administration record, reads new and changed orders verified overnight, notes doses due, held or awaiting pharmacy verification, and plans the timing of the morning pass around tests and meals.

error.defect_description: A newly changed order is overlooked.

evidence.note: eMAR was used by 54% of Ontario hospitals in 2020/21 (src5); others printed MARs from the pharmacy system. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Withdraw the morning doses from the dispensing cabinet
steps.description: The nurse logs into the automated dispensing cabinet with a fingerprint, selects the patient, removes each due dose from its pocket or the patient's drawer, enters a blind count for controlled drugs, and notes any dose that is not stocked or not yet profiled by pharmacy.

error.defect_description: Wrong drug or strength taken from a look-alike pocket.

control.basis: Narcotic Control Regulations and hospital controlled-drug policy: counted withdrawal of controlled substances

next.condition: a dose is missing or not profiled

evidence.note: 89% of Canadian hospitals used automated dispensing cabinets in 2020/21 (src5). Wait is the queue at the cabinet at 08:00, when all nurses on the unit start the same pass; author's estimate.

steps.name: Call pharmacy about a missing dose
steps.description: The nurse checks the patient's drawer and the cabinet again, then phones pharmacy to ask whether the order is verified and when the dose will come, and notes the delay on the medication record.

evidence.note: Missing doses on about 10% of patient days is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Pharmacy sends the missing dose
steps.description: A pharmacy technician finds the order in the pharmacy queue, picks or prepares the dose once a pharmacist has verified the order, labels it and sends it by pneumatic tube or carries it to the unit.

error.defect_description: Dose sent to the wrong unit.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; pharmacy verification turnaround is measured in the order verification workflow.

steps.name: Prepare the doses at the medication cart
steps.description: The nurse checks each dose against the record (drug, dose, route, time), crushes or splits tablets where ordered, draws up injections and dilutes IV push doses, checks expiry dates and allergies, and labels anything drawn up away from the bedside.

error.defect_description: Dose prepared wrongly after an interruption.

evidence.note: Interruptions occurred in over half of administrations and each raised the clinical error rate by 12.7% (src2). Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Give and document the morning doses at the bedside
steps.description: At the bedside the nurse confirms identity with two identifiers, scans the armband and each dose where barcode scanning is in place, checks vital signs or blood glucose before drugs that need them, gives the doses, watches the patient swallow, and documents each administration in the record.

error.defect_description: Wrong time, omitted dose or undocumented dose.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada ROP: client identification with two identifiers before giving medications

next.condition: high-alert drug due (insulin, heparin, opioid infusion)

evidence.note: A quarter of observed administrations had a clinical error even without interruption (src2), most of them minor timing or procedural errors. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Independent double check of a high-alert dose
steps.description: The nurse asks a second nurse to check the order, drug, concentration, dose calculation and pump settings for insulin, heparin or an opioid infusion without seeing the first nurse's working, and both sign the record.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada ROP: high-alert medications; ISMP Canada independent double check recommendation

evidence.note: ISMP Canada found lack of an independent double check in many IV administration incidents (src3). The wait is finding a free second nurse; author's estimate.

steps.name: Program the infusion pump and hang the IV medication
steps.description: The nurse traces the line from bag to patient, selects the drug in the smart pump library, enters rate and volume, confirms the program against the label and order, starts the infusion and documents it.

error.defect_description: Pump programmed with the wrong rate or line.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada ROP: infusion pump safety

evidence.note: About 1 in 6 IV incidents involved pump programming or accessories (src3). Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Give the midday doses
steps.description: Around noon the nurse withdraws, checks and gives the midday doses, often insulin with lunch after a glucose check, and documents them; for stable patients this nurse is often a registered practical nurse.

error.defect_description: Insulin given without matching meal intake.

next.condition: patient asks for an as-needed dose

evidence.note: Author's estimate of a typical four-pass day (08:00, 12:00, 17:00, 22:00).

steps.name: Give an as-needed dose on request
steps.description: When the patient asks for pain, nausea or sleep medicine, the nurse assesses the symptom score, checks the last dose time and limits on the record, withdraws the dose (with a count for opioids), gives it and documents the reason.

error.defect_description: Dose given too early after the previous dose.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; the wait is the patient waiting for the nurse to come free.

steps.name: Reassess the effect of the as-needed dose
steps.description: Thirty to sixty minutes later the nurse returns, asks about the pain or nausea score, checks sedation after an opioid, and records the effect.

error.defect_description: Reassessment not done or not recorded.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Give the late-afternoon doses
steps.description: Around 17:00 the nurse withdraws, checks and gives the late-afternoon doses, checking blood pressure, heart rate or blood glucose before drugs with hold parameters.

error.defect_description: Dose given outside the hold parameter.

next.condition: a dose must be held and the prescriber called

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Hold a dose and page the prescriber
steps.description: When the patient's blood pressure is low, the patient is fasting for a test or vomiting, the nurse holds the dose, pages the physician with the reading and the question, and records the held dose.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Prescriber answers and changes the order
steps.description: The hospitalist calls back, decides whether to give, hold or change the dose, and writes or gives a verbal order that the nurse reads back and records for pharmacy verification.

control.basis: Ontario Public Hospitals Act, Regulation 965: orders by an authorized practitioner; verbal orders read back and countersigned

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Count controlled drugs and hand over at shift change
steps.description: At 19:00 the outgoing and oncoming nurses reconcile the unit's controlled-drug count and review which doses are due, held or late for each patient; the per-patient share of this work is small.

error.defect_description: Count discrepancy not resolved before the outgoing nurse leaves.

control.basis: Narcotic Control Regulations and hospital controlled-drug policy: count at each shift change

evidence.note: Many units with dispensing cabinets count only cabinet discrepancies; author's estimate.

steps.name: Give the bedtime doses
steps.description: Around 21:00 to 22:00 the night nurse withdraws, checks and gives bedtime doses such as anticoagulants, sedatives and evening insulin, and documents them.

error.defect_description: Dose omitted while the night nurse covers more patients.

next.condition: overnight IV antibiotic or as-needed dose

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Give an overnight dose
steps.description: During the night the nurse hangs a scheduled IV antibiotic or gives an as-needed dose for pain or sleep, documenting it in the record.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Check the 24-hour medication record
steps.description: Before morning the night nurse reviews the record for the past day, looks for doses not signed for, documents reasons for late or omitted doses, and reports a medication incident if a dose was missed, wrong or given to the wrong patient.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of about 130 reported medication incidents a month (about a fifth of the 600 incident reports a month in the organisation file) over 18,500 patient days.

steps.name: Report the medication incident
steps.description: The nurse assesses the patient, informs the physician, enters a report in the safety incident system describing the drug, dose, error type and harm, and tells the charge nurse; the manager follows up through incident management.

control.basis: Ontario Public Hospitals Act, Regulation 965: disclosure of critical incidents; hospital incident reporting policy

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Missing dose
exceptions.description: A due dose is not in the cabinet or drawer, usually because the order is not yet verified or the patient-specific dose has not arrived; the nurse calls pharmacy and the dose is given late.

exceptions.name: High-alert medication
exceptions.description: Insulin, heparin or an opioid infusion needs an independent double check by a second nurse.

exceptions.name: Held dose
exceptions.description: A dose is held for low blood pressure, fasting or vomiting and the prescriber is paged.

exceptions.name: Medication incident
exceptions.description: An omitted, wrong or wrong-patient dose is found and reported.

benchmarks.unit: share of nurse working time (24.5% after barcode administration)
benchmarks.population: Medical, surgical and ICU nurses at one 735-bed US tertiary hospital, 2005

benchmarks.unit: share of administrations with at least one interruption (reported as more than half)

evidence.note: Each interruption raised clinical errors by 12.7%.

benchmarks.unit: minutes from prescriber writing an order to nurse giving the first dose

benchmarks.population: CSHP Hospital Pharmacy in Canada survey

evidence.note: 25% nationally; 61% print MARs from the pharmacy system.

pain_points.description: All nurses on a unit start the 08:00 pass at once, so they queue at the dispensing cabinet and late doses pile up.

evidence.note: Author's observation of common practice.

pain_points.description: Interruptions during preparation and administration are frequent and raise the error rate.
Doses missing from the cabinet or drawer because pharmacy has not yet verified or delivered them cause phone calls and late doses.

evidence.note: Most Canadian pharmacies are not open 24/7 and cannot review all orders before administration (src5); order-to-first-dose took a median of 300 minutes (src6).

pain_points.description: Finding a free second nurse for high-alert double checks delays insulin and infusions; skipped checks appear in incident reports.

sources.title: Impact of Barcode Medication Administration Technology on How Nurses Spend Their Time On Clinical Care
sources.publisher: AMIA Annual Symposium Proceedings (Poon EG, Keohane C and others)
sources.supports: Time-motion study, 232 two-hour sessions on medical, surgical and intensive care units of a 735-bed hospital: nurses spent 26.5% of their time on medication administration before barcode administration and 24.5% after (not significant); direct care unrelated to medications 20.1% and 23.7%.

sources.title: Association of interruptions with an increased risk and severity of medication administration errors (PSNet summary of Westbrook JI and others, Arch Intern Med 2010)
sources.supports: Interruptions occurred in more than half of observed medication administrations; each interruption was associated with a 12.1% increase in procedural failures and a 12.7% increase in clinical errors; administrations without interruption still had a 25% clinical error rate.

sources.title: Intravenous Medication Safety: A Multi-Incident Analysis (ISMP Canada Safety Bulletin vol. 20 no. 7)
sources.publisher: Institute for Safe Medication Practices Canada
sources.supports: 1,583 IV medication incidents from Canadian reporting systems (2015-2018); about one-third were administration errors (wrong patient, drug, dose, route or rate); lack of an independent double check and over-reliance on smart pumps and barcode technology contributed; about 1 in 6 involved pump programming or accessories; MAR and pharmacy label mismatches and portering delays also contributed.

sources.title: Required Organizational Practices 2021 Handbook
sources.publisher: Accreditation Canada (copy hosted by Vitalite Health Network)
sources.supports: Accreditation Canada ROPs include client identification with two identifiers, information transfer at care transitions, medication reconciliation at care transitions (best possible medication history at admission), concentrated electrolytes, heparin safety, high-alert medications, infusion pump safety, narcotics safety, falls prevention, pressure ulcer prevention and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis.

sources.title: Hospital Pharmacy in Canada Survey 2020/21 Report
sources.supports: 142 hospital pharmacy departments (hospitals of 50+ acute beds): pharmacies open an average 86 hours a week (96 for hospitals over 500 beds, 89 for 201-500 beds); only 9% open 24/7 (7 of 13 in Ontario); pharmacists review orders before the first dose in most (50-99%) areas in 76% of hospitals; only 2-3% review routine orders before after-hours night cupboard, ADC or ward stock access, 17% before the order reaches the MAR; 89% use automated dispensing cabinets; 77% use centralized unit dose; 19% had operational CPOE; 61% print MARs from the pharmacy system and 25% use eMAR (54% in Ontario); technical staff check patient-specific IV admixtures in 72% and ADC replenishment in 97% of hospitals.

sources.title: Decreasing Medication Turnaround Time with Digital Scanning Technology in a Canadian Health Region
sources.publisher: Canadian Journal of Hospital Pharmacy (Neville H, Nodwell L, Alsharif S)
sources.supports: Two hospital sites, 548 orders audited in 2011: median time from prescriber writing the order to pharmacy verification fell from 143 to 93 minutes after scanned orders replaced the previous transmission; median time from order to nurse administration 315 and 300 minutes (not significant).

assumptions: Loaded costs come from the organisation file. The medicine RN and RPN roles stand for all inpatient nurses in the steps; their costs are the same as the surgical, mental health, postpartum and paediatric nurses' and close to the ICU nurses'.
A typical patient day has four scheduled passes, an as-needed dose on about two-thirds of days, an IV dose on about four in ten days and a high-alert drug on one in five days (author's estimates).
About 70-75 minutes of nurse time per patient day, which is roughly a quarter of the RN and RPN time per inpatient day in an Ontario community hospital, matching the 24.5-26.5% share in src1.
The medication incident rate here (0.7% of patient days) is the reported rate. Observational studies find errors in a quarter of administrations (src2), most of them minor and never reported.
No cycle-time benchmark exists for a patient day of medications; the simulated elapsed time (about 22 hours from the first review to the overnight record check) follows the pass schedule.
The organisation file does not list the hospitalist or pharmacy technician for this process; both are added from the organisation's role list for held-dose calls and missing-dose deliveries.
